content.summary_of_the_paper:
MDP for dynamical systems -- application to transportation and to wind turbines.
The submission considers acting load estimation, which is the problem of estimating the input for a system to achieve the observed output. The submission proposes to reformulate this problem into a POMDP problem, and thus can be solved by existing model-based or model-free POMDP methods. Empirical results are provided to support the proposed framework.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Sterngths

Well written, applications in mind. The main idea is clearly demonstrated. 
Thorough empirical results are provided supporting the proposed method. 

Weaknesses

First of all, the motivation of the submission is unclear. For example, why does the submission formulate the problem in to a POMDP emphasizing the dynamics of the states instead of a supervised learning problem? Even for a time-dependent problem we can still leverage supervised learning methods. Also, what are the benefits of formulating the problem into a POMDP? There is little discussion on the benefits of doing so except being able to leverage existing POMDP methods. 

Second, the contribution of the submission is a little restricted. The main contribution seems to be proposing that one can use POMDP methods to solve the input estimation problem. I am wondering what might be the major novelty of CEM used in the submission?
content.summary_of_the_review: The submission proposed a new formulation of the input estimation problem. However, the motivation and contribution of the submission are not very clear.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The objective of this paper is, given a model of dynamical system with stochastic transitions and emissions, and an output sequence, to infer the input sequence that is most likely to have given rise to that output sequence, given the model.

The approach is to formulate an optimization problem, which seeks to find the control sequence u_1, ... u_n that, when fed into the dynamical system, generates an output sequence hat(x)_1, ..., hat(x)_n that has minimal distance from observed output sequence x_1, ..., x_n.  

The optimization problem is solved with a stochastic local search method called CEM, which uses sampling techniques inspired by evolutionary search mechanisms.

The method is demonstrated to generate accurate results in several problems, including one in which the dynamics model has been estimated form data.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is clearly written and the problem is useful and important.

The formulation, however, seems to be much more complex than necessary.  This is a relatively straightforward optimization problem.  Treating it as a POMDP doesn't seem to generate any additional insight, and the CEM method, although it is often used to optimize the parameters in a policy, is a general-purpose optimization method.

An additional substantial weakness is that the method is not empirically compared against any others.  It seems unlikely that no-one has tried to solve this inverse problem before and it would be useful to compare this method directly against previous ones.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clear and the methods are described in what seems like sufficient detail for replication.  

However, because the optimization algorithm is itself stochastic, it would be important to run experiments to see how much variability there is in the solutions you are obtaining, because CEM can be subject to problems of local optima.
content.summary_of_the_review: Problems of the type tackled here could have importance in many real application situations, but they seem to call for a much more straightforward approach.  The connection to machine learning of any kind, and especially to representation learning is quite weak and makes this paper really not suited to the conference.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper views the problem of input system estimation in dynamical systems as a reinforcement learning problem. The idea is that with either known or learnt dynamics, to run CEM-style MBRL to recover the input (u) that produce the measurements (x) that best match the data. The optimization approach used is a CEM-based one. The performance of this approach is measured on a simulated known structural system, a road and railway profile system and a real world complex wind turbine system.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 

To my knowledge, this approach is novel and attempts to solve an important problem of input estimation. This is an interesting problem and the solution is elegant and has potential to be directly useful for the downstream tasks. The method is able to learn the input pretty well based on the results, which are also presented in a clear and coherent fashion. Overall this is a simple approach to a difficult problem. 

Weaknesses: 

I think a major weakness is how this would compare to more traditional or non-RL based approaches for input estimation. It would be good to include some baselines or comparisons about this. Another consideration that is important is how sample efficient/data efficient this approach is (or what is the time complexity)? I think benchmarking the data efficiency would be important as well. It would be good to also understand how this approach compares to differentiable solvers such as Pineda et al. [1]. 

[1] Pineda, Luis et al., Theseus: A Library for Differentiable Nonlinear Optimization., 2022.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Paper is well presented, writing and experiments are of good quality and to my knowledge this is novel.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall this is a simple solution to an interesting and challenging problem. The paper presents the solution in a easy to understand manner, and the experiments do support the papers claims, but would be much stronger if compared against baselines and benchmarked (see weaknesses).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addresses the problem of input inference/parameter identification from measured output for a known or learned dynamical systems. By formulating the input inference problem as a POMDP, the paper adopted the standard cross-entropy method (CEM) to solve for a policy representing the sequence of estimated parameters, whose resulting cumulative rewards (depicted as the error between the inferred and observed outputs) are minimized. The main contribution is the contextualized CEM approach in the reformulated POMDP, and its application in a simulated 10-DOF structural system as the experimental results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
+ The general idea of this paper is well written with clear motivation and good overview about the high level idea of the algorithm.
+ A good coverage of the related work in multiple relevant fields.
+ The idea of reformulating the input inference problem into the POMDP framework is interesting and using CEM seems to be a reasonable solution
 
Weakness:
- The technical contribution seems rather incremental as the paper simply implements the CEM algorithm into a POMDP formulation without novel results on the theory part, and most of the proofs directly follow the standard theoretical results from the well-know CEM method.
- While the discussion on the application to iteratively learned dynamics is interesting, the presented additional result simply uses deep learning model as a replacement to the known dynamics model, without addressing the resulting challenge such as the convergence of CEM with an iteratively learned dynamics model.
- The experimental results are given in different simulation examples, yet there is no comparison results from other baseline approaches.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The studied problem of input inference via POMDP itself is an interesting perspective and is very relevant to the ICLR community. The paper is in overall well written to highlight the motivation, existing challenges, and the adapted approach of the CEM framework. With that being said, however, the presented framework seems to be a simple contextualization of the existing CEM framework, with incremental changes of the defined objective function to adapt to the input inference problem. The main proofs of the convergence and algorithm performance is natural unleashed from standard CEM framework, making the contribution too incremental. Please see detailed comments as follows.

- Contribution and Novelty: while the presented motivation is clear that focuses on the reformulated POMDP to address input inference, the reviewer feels the contribution is quite incremental, given that Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2 mainly follow the standard CEM approach as well as the proofs. There is little contribution in terms of the theoretical aspect.

- Quality: as a follow-up comment from above, the challenge of input inference under unmodelled dynamics is not well addressed by the contextualized CEM approach. For example, there has been extensive new results, e.g. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), on model-based reinforcement learning for efficient RL tasks, which seems also proper in the studied input inference problem. The interesting tension comes from how to show convergence with the iteratively learned dynamics when it is not fully modelled. In this paper, however, the dynamics, regardless of given or modelled online, is treated the same as a standard component in the CEM framework. It is not well justified that why CEM is used here together with the POMDP formulation.

- Experimental results: from the experiment section, there is no comparison results from other baseline approaches and with only the performance of the standard CEM algorithm. Authors are encouraged to provide more comparative analysis with other similar approaches, e.g. model-based RL or MPC approaches.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper mainly follows the standard approach of CEM with the incremental contribution in reformulating the input inference problem into a POMDP, yet it is not well justified why CEM would be the best choice in solving the reformulated problem. On the other hand, the experimental results lack comparison to other baseline approaches which makes it difficult to evaluate how well the algorithm performs. Authors are encouraged to address the comments in the future version of the paper.
